prompt: What do the people who decide a release read first in a test report?
hint: Two questions.

choices.text: The pass rate, and how it moved since the last release
choices.why: A rate cannot say which failures matter, and boxoffice's fell while 1.1 fixed two defects.

choices.text: Whether to ship, and the risk if we do
choices.why: Right: everything else is evidence for those two answers.

choices.text: How many cases were written and run
choices.why: That measures effort, which nobody deciding a release needs.

choices.text: The list of defects, each with its id
choices.why: Ids mean nothing to the manager; the risks go in her words.

prompt: The pass rate went from 64% on 1.0 to 59% on 1.1, although 1.1 fixed two defects and broke one. Why did it fall?
hint: Look at the cells that were empty on 1.0.

choices.text: 1.1 broke more things than it fixed
choices.why: It fixed two and broke one; the rate is not counting that.

choices.text: Three new cases joined, each checking a defect already found
choices.why: Right: a case written from a defect fails on the day it is added.

choices.text: The 1.1 run was done in a hurry and missed passes
choices.why: Every result in the 1.1 column records what 1.1 does.

choices.text: Blocked cases were counted as failures
choices.why: No case in either run was blocked.

prompt: Match each reader to what they read of the same run.
hint: The table in section 01.

pairs.right: The failure messages and the defect report
Results by status and by area
One page: can we release, and what happens if we do

right_distractors: The effort: hours and cases written

prompt: Which sentence belongs in the risk part of a page for the theatre's manager?
hint: Her words, not the tester's.

choices.text: TC-10 failed on 1.1
choices.why: A case id means nothing to her; she cannot weigh it against a delay.

choices.text: R5 has one failure among its three cases, all of them run on build 1.1
choices.why: Accurate, and still in the tester's vocabulary rather than the theatre's.

choices.text: Two student tickets for Hamlet cost R$ 160,00, not R$ 80,00
choices.why: Right: who is hurt and by how much, in reais.

choices.text: The discount function ignores the student flag since the 1.1 edit
choices.why: That is the developer's explanation, for the defect report.

prompt: The manager reads the page and decides to release 1.1 with the misspelt message still open. What is the tester's job now?
hint: Who decides a release?

choices.text: Refuse the release until every defect is fixed
choices.why: The tester informs the decision; holding it is not theirs to do.

choices.text: Mark the message defect as fixed so the exit criteria hold
choices.why: That falsifies the record the page was built from.

choices.text: None beyond the page: she decided with the risk in front of her
choices.why: Right: a known defect released on purpose is a decision, not a surprise.

choices.text: Rewrite the page so the message sounds more serious
choices.why: The page states the risk as it is; inflating it to win is the same fault as softening it.

prompt: What is JUnit XML, as section 02 describes it?
hint: Who writes it, and who reads it?

choices.text: The report format of Java unit tests, and nothing else
choices.why: It began there and spread to almost every runner, manual results included.

choices.text: A results format most tools write and read
choices.why: Right: a de facto common language, never published as a standard.

choices.text: A formal standard every tool implements in exactly the same way
choices.why: Nobody published it as one, so tools differ at the edges.

choices.text: Allure's own folder of results
choices.why: Allure has its own result format and can also read this one.

prompt: Match what is inside a testcase element to the result it records.
hint: The table in section 02.

pairs.right: It ran and the check did not hold
It could not run to the end: something unexpected broke

right_distractors: It was blocked by another defect

prompt: In results-1.0.xml, how many cases came out as skipped?
hint: The second line of the file.

prompt: A team's manual results include blocked cases, and they convert them to JUnit XML. What does section 02 say they have to do?
hint: Which element is blocked?

choices.text: Choose a mapping and write it down
choices.why: Right: the format has no blocked, and two converters choosing differently give two counts of what was tested.

choices.text: Write them as failure, since the case did not pass
choices.why: Failure says the behaviour is wrong; nobody saw the behaviour.

choices.text: Leave them out of the file altogether
choices.why: Then the file says fewer cases exist than the run holds.

choices.text: Use the blocked element the format reserves for them
choices.why: There is none: nothing, failure, error and skipped are the four.

prompt: to_junit.py puts each case's requirement in classname. What does that buy?
hint: How do most readers group cases?

choices.text: The format requires a requirement id in that attribute
choices.why: It requires a name for a group; what the group is, the converter decides.

choices.text: Results shown by requirement
choices.why: Right: R6 with four cases, R5 with three, R9 with one.

choices.text: It makes the file valid XML
choices.why: The file would be valid with any text there.

choices.text: It stops two cases from having the same name
choices.why: The case id in the name already does that.

prompt: In JUnit XML, a testcase element with nothing inside it records that the case ___.
hint: Most lines of results-1.1.xml look like this.

prompt: Does Allure run the tests it reports on?
hint: Where do the results come from?

choices.text: Yes, it runs them and then draws the report
choices.why: The tests run in the team's own framework; Allure only reads what they leave.

choices.text: No; it reads results the tests leave
choices.why: Right: an adapter writes them as the tests run, or a runner writes JUnit XML, and Allure builds pages from them.

choices.text: Only JUnit tests, written in Java
choices.why: Adapters exist for the common frameworks in several languages.

choices.text: It records manual testing by watching the browser
choices.why: It reads result files; nothing in it watches a person test.

prompt: A team's Allure report shows today's results and no history. What is the likeliest reason?
hint: What does a report need to know about the past?

choices.text: History is shown for manual tests only
choices.why: Allure is fed by automated runs; history works the same for them.

choices.text: The tests were not labelled with features and stories
choices.why: Labels group the tests; they have nothing to do with the past.

choices.text: Earlier results were not kept for it
choices.why: Right: without the earlier results the report knows only today.

choices.text: The XML did not carry a time for every case
choices.why: Times are durations within one run, not a record of earlier runs.

prompt: Instead of writing a page, Ana sends the theatre's manager the link to an Allure report of the 1.1 run. What goes wrong?
hint: Whose job ends up done by whom?

choices.text: She learns to read it, or decides by the colour of a chart
choices.why: Right: the tester's job is handed upwards, or skipped.

choices.text: Nothing: the report holds every result and its evidence
choices.why: It holds the evidence and not the answer to "can we ship".

choices.text: The link will not open outside the CI server
choices.why: The report is a static site and opens anywhere; the trouble is what it says.

choices.text: Allure leaves manual results out of the 1.1 run
choices.why: This run came from a spreadsheet anyway; the problem would remain with every result in.

prompt: Put these rows of the one-page report in the order section 04 gives them.
hint: What does a reader who stops after one line need?
items: What happens if it is released as it is
The plan's exit criteria, each yes or no
trap: The numbers are evidence, so they come last.

prompt: Why does the page name the misspelt message and the phone layout in a row of their own?
hint: What would happen to the price in the same list?

choices.text: They are too small to be worth naming at all
choices.why: They are named, so a later release with them open is a decision.

choices.text: Beside a typo, the price would look small
choices.why: Right: apart, each is weighed at its own size, and none is hidden.

choices.text: The plan says layout defects go in a separate report
choices.why: The plan says nothing of the kind; the order is about the reader.

choices.text: They were found by other testers
choices.why: Who found a defect does not decide where it goes on the page.

prompt: Why does the page quote the exit criteria from lesson 1's plan instead of the tester's view of whether 1.1 is good enough?
hint: When were they written?

choices.text: Because a tester's view is not allowed in a report
choices.why: The page carries judgement, severity among it; the criteria anchor it.

choices.text: So the page is longer and looks more thorough
choices.why: The page is kept short on purpose.

choices.text: Because the criteria pass, which makes the release safe
choices.why: Two of the three fail on 1.1.

choices.text: They were agreed before any case ran
choices.why: Right: nobody says the bar moved at the end, and "can we ship" becomes a comparison everybody signed up to in advance.

prompt: A shop's test report opens with "312 cases, 97% passed". The failing 3% include every case for card payment. What should its first line say instead?
hint: What does a reader who stops there need?

choices.text: "97% passed, up from 95% last release"
choices.why: A better rate, and the reader still does not know that nobody can pay.

choices.text: "Not ready: customers cannot pay by card"
choices.why: Right: the answer, and the consequence that decides it, in the business's words.

choices.text: "Ten payment cases failed; see the attached XML for details"
choices.why: Cases and files are evidence; the reader still has to work out the answer.

choices.text: "Testing is mostly complete, with some concerns"
choices.why: Softened wording is read as a yes.

prompt: Which of these belong on the one page for the theatre's manager? Choose every one that applies.
hint: Section 04's rows, and what it left out.

choices.text: What was not tested, such as the confirmation link
choices.why: Right: a reader who assumes everything was tested decides differently.

choices.text: What changed since 1.0
choices.why: Right: two things fixed and one broken, as news.

choices.text: What would change the answer
choices.why: Right: the defects to fix and the suite to run again.

choices.text: The result of each of the seventeen cases
choices.why: One link away; the page says what they mean.

choices.text: The hours spent testing 1.1
choices.why: Effort, which nobody deciding a release needs.

prompt: Run A's only failure is a misspelt message. Run B's only failure is the price. What do their pass rates say about the difference?
hint: Count, then think about what the count leaves out.

choices.text: Nothing: with the same number of cases, the rates are equal
choices.why: Right: a rate counts failures and cannot weigh them.

choices.text: Run B's rate is lower, since a price failure counts double
choices.why: No rate weighs failures; each one counts once.

choices.text: Run A's rate is lower, since messages have more cases
choices.why: Both runs have one failure; the rate cannot see which.

choices.text: That run B is ready to release
choices.why: One failing price case is exactly what holds a release.
